public_rationale: The checkable core of the claim is that Kosinski's study did not prove that GPT-3 had a general theory of mind. That holds. Tomer Ullman tested the same tasks and found that small changes, which should not matter to anyone with theory of mind, reversed the models' successes. He concluded that current LLMs do not pass theory-of-mind tests. One caveat matters: Kosinski did not just reuse the textbook items. Research assistants wrote 20 new variants to reduce training-data exposure. So Marcus overstates how well represented the exact tests were. His conclusion still stands.
limitations: Whether a study 'proves' something is partly a judgment call.
'The study doesn't tell us much' is evaluative and is not scored.
Marcus's contamination premise is only partly accurate, given Kosinski's bespoke tasks.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Kosinski's study does not prove that GPT-3 has abstracted a generalized theory of mind, because its tests are well represented in training data.

statement.excerpt: But without a test that goes significantly beyond what is so well-represented in the training regime, the study doesn’t tell us much. Certainly it doesn’t prove that the system has abstracted a generalized version of theory of mind.

our_interpretation: 'The study' is Kosinski's February 2023 preprint, 'Theory of Mind May Have Spontaneously Emerged in Large Language Models'.
The checkable core: did that study's evidence establish a general theory of mind in GPT-3? Robust failures on small, theory-of-mind-preserving changes to the same tasks would show it did not.
'Doesn't tell us much' is evaluative and is not scored on its own.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence available by early 2023 that the models' success on Kosinski's tasks did not hold under minor changes that should not matter to an entity with theory of mind.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that the study's tasks were novel and that performance held up robustly under perturbations, so that it did show general theory of mind.

evidence.excerpt:
We show that the original reported successes
are susceptible to small perturbations that shouldn’t matter to an entity that has ToM.
evidence.explanation: Independent tests show that Kosinski's reported successes break under small, theory-of-mind-preserving changes. So the study did not establish a general theory of mind.

evidence.excerpt:
The current work (as well as related work such as (14))
suggests the premise of the dilemma is unfounded – current LLMs do not pass ToM tests.
evidence.explanation: Ullman concludes that the models do not really pass theory-of-mind tests once the tests are varied. This matches Marcus's view that the study does not prove a general theory of mind.

evidence.excerpt:
As GPT-3.5 may have encountered the original task in its training, hypothesis-blind research
assistants (RAs) prepared 20 bespoke Unexpected Contents Task tasks.
evidence.explanation: Kosinski did try to control for training-data exposure with newly written variants. This weakens Marcus's premise that the tests were simply memorized, though the variants keep the classic structure.
